title_it: reFX rilascia Rippler, un sintetizzatore di modellazione fisica a doppio strato
summary_it: Il nuovo plug-in combina l’emulazione acustica basata su risonatore con la sintesi sottrattiva, con un prezzo di lancio di 99 dollari. reFX ha rilasciato Rippler, un nuovo plugin che combina...
content_it: Il nuovo plug-in combina l’emulazione acustica basata su risonatore con la sintesi sottrattiva, con un prezzo di lancio di 99 dollari. reFX ha rilasciato Rippler, un nuovo plugin che combina la modellazione fisica con la sintesi sottrattiva su due livelli indipendenti. Il plugin è ora disponibile per macOS 10.13 e versioni successive, che supporta sia i processori Apple Silicon che Intel, e per Windows 10 e versioni successive, nei formati VST, Audio Units e AAX. Rippler è progettato per generare timbri acustici e semiacustici modellando il comportamento fisico di strumenti come corde, tubi, membrane e campane, quindi modellando il suono risultante con strumenti di filtraggio e modulazione convenzionali. La struttura a doppio strato consente di fondere o sovrapporre due catene di segnali di questo tipo all'interno di una singola patch, insieme a una serie di effetti, controlli delle prestazioni e contenuti preimpostati. Ogni livello inizia con uno stadio di eccitazione, che offre una scelta di suoni incorporati, l'opzione di importare campioni utente e un ingresso sidechain. Il segnale dell'eccitatore, insieme a un generatore di rumore dedicato, alimenta due risonatori: il nucleo del motore di modellazione fisica di Rippler. I risonatori si basano su 12 modelli destinati a rappresentare diverse sorgenti sonore acustiche, inclusi i tipi di corda, trave, campana, membrana, piastra, pelle di tamburo, djembe, vibrafono e marimba, insieme a modelli a tubo aperto e chiuso. Una modalità manuale aggiunge un generatore di sintesi additiva. I due risonatori possono funzionare in parallelo o in serie, con la possibilità di alimentarli l'uno nell'altro. Due oscillatori possono essere introdotti insieme ai risonatori per fondere elementi sintetizzati e modellati all'interno dello stesso strato, e due filtri - che offrono 27 tipi che spaziano da configurazioni standard passa-basso, passa-alto, passa-banda e notch, filtri vintage e stile ladder e un filtro vocale di spostamento delle formanti - modellano l'uscita combinata. La modulazione è gestita da quattro LFO e quattro tipi di inviluppo (ADSR, AHD, DADSR e DAHDSR), integrati da generatori casuali, velocità, chiave e sorgente aftertouch
title_en: reFX releases Rippler, a dual‑layer physical modelling synthesiser
summary_en: New plugin combines resonator‑based acoustic emulation with subtractive synthesis, launching at an introductory price of $99. reFX has released Rippler, a new plugin that combines ...
content_en: New plugin combines resonator‑based acoustic emulation with subtractive synthesis, launching at an introductory price of $99. reFX has released Rippler, a new plugin that combines physical modelling with subtractive synthesis across two independent layers. The plugin is available now for macOS 10.13 and later, supporting both Apple Silicon and Intel processors, and for Windows 10 and above, in VST, Audio Units and AAX formats. Rippler is designed to generate acoustic and semi‑acoustic timbres by modelling the physical behaviour of instruments such as strings, tubes, membranes and bells, then shaping the resulting sound with conventional filtering and modulation tools. The dual‑layer structure allows two such signal chains to be blended or layered within a single patch, alongside a set of effects, performance controls and preset content. Each layer begins with an exciter stage, which offers a choice of built‑in sounds, the option to import user samples, and a sidechain input. The exciter signal, together with a dedicated noise generator, feeds into two resonators – the core of Rippler's physical modelling engine. The resonators draw on 12 models intended to represent different acoustic sound sources, including string, beam, bell, membrane, plate, drumhead, djembe, vibraphone and marimba types, along with open and closed tube models. A manual mode adds an additive synthesis generator. The two resonators can be run in parallel or in series, with the option to feed one into the other. Two oscillators can be introduced alongside the resonators to blend synthesised and modelled elements within the same layer, and two filters – offering 27 types spanning standard low‑pass, high‑pass, band‑pass and notch configurations, vintage and ladder‑style filters, and a formant‑shifting vowel filter – shape the combined output. Modulation is handled by four LFOs and four envelope types (ADSR, AHD, DADSR and DAHDSR), supplemented by random generators, velocity, key and aftertouch sources, four assignable macros, and MPE compatibility. Each layer carries its own effects chain, selectable from 13 processor types, and a master chain processes the combined output of both layers. An onboard arpeggiator and sequencer includes modifier lanes that can add or subtract pitch and velocity from a played pattern. Find out more on the reFX website. After September 13, the price goes up to $129. content_es: El nuevo complemento combina la emulación acústica basada en resonador con síntesis sustractiva y se lanza a un precio de lanzamiento de $99. reFX ha lanzado Rippler, un nuevo complemento que combina modelado físico con síntesis sustractiva en dos capas independientes. El complemento ya está disponible para macOS 10.13 y versiones posteriores, y es compatible con procesadores Apple Silicon e Intel, y para Windows 10 y versiones posteriores, en formatos VST, Audio Units y AAX. Rippler está diseñado para generar timbres acústicos y semiacústicos modelando el comportamiento físico de instrumentos como cuerdas, tubos, membranas y campanas, y luego dando forma al sonido resultante con herramientas convencionales de filtrado y modulación. La estructura de doble capa permite combinar o superponer dos cadenas de señales en un solo parche, junto con un conjunto de efectos, controles de interpretación y contenido preestablecido. Cada capa comienza con una etapa de excitación, que ofrece una selección de sonidos integrados, la opción de importar muestras de usuario y una entrada de cadena lateral. La señal del excitador, junto con un generador de ruido dedicado, alimenta dos resonadores: el núcleo del motor de modelado físico de Rippler. Los resonadores se basan en 12 modelos destinados a representar diferentes fuentes de sonido acústico, incluidos tipos de cuerda, viga, campana, membrana, plato, parche, djembé, vibráfono y marimba, junto con modelos de tubo abierto y cerrado. Un modo manual agrega un generador de síntesis aditiva. Los dos resonadores pueden funcionar en paralelo o en serie, con la opción de alimentar uno al otro. Se pueden introducir dos osciladores junto con los resonadores para combinar elementos sintetizados y modelados dentro de la misma capa, y dos filtros, que ofrecen 27 tipos que abarcan configuraciones estándar de paso bajo, paso alto, paso de banda y muesca, filtros vintage y de estilo escalera, y un filtro vocal de cambio de formantes, dan forma a la salida combinada. La modulación es manejada por cuatro LFO y cuatro tipos de envolvente (ADSR, AHD, DADSR y DAHDSR), complementados con generadores aleatorios, velocidad, clave y fuente de aftertouch.

content_fr: Le nouveau plugin combine une émulation acoustique basée sur un résonateur avec une synthèse soustractive, lancé au prix de lancement de 99 $. reFX a publié Rippler, un nouveau plugin qui combine la modélisation physique et la synthèse soustractive sur deux couches indépendantes. Le plugin est désormais disponible pour macOS 10.13 et versions ultérieures, prenant en charge les processeurs Apple Silicon et Intel, et pour Windows 10 et versions ultérieures, aux formats VST, Audio Units et AAX. Rippler est conçu pour générer des timbres acoustiques et semi-acoustiques en modélisant le comportement physique d'instruments tels que des cordes, des tubes, des membranes et des cloches, puis en façonnant le son résultant avec des outils de filtrage et de modulation conventionnels. La structure à double couche permet de mélanger ou de superposer deux de ces chaînes de signaux dans un seul patch, aux côtés d'un ensemble d'effets, de commandes de performances et de contenus prédéfinis. Chaque couche commence par un étage d'excitation, qui offre un choix de sons intégrés, la possibilité d'importer des échantillons utilisateur et une entrée sidechain. Le signal d'excitation, associé à un générateur de bruit dédié, alimente deux résonateurs – le cœur du moteur de modélisation physique de Rippler. Les résonateurs s'appuient sur 12 modèles destinés à représenter différentes sources sonores acoustiques, notamment les types de cordes, poutres, cloches, membranes, plaques, peaux de tambour, djembé, vibraphone et marimba, ainsi que des modèles à tubes ouverts et fermés. Un mode manuel ajoute un générateur de synthèse additive. Les deux résonateurs peuvent fonctionner en parallèle ou en série, avec la possibilité de s'alimenter l'un dans l'autre. Deux oscillateurs peuvent être introduits à côté des résonateurs pour mélanger des éléments synthétisés et modélisés au sein de la même couche, et deux filtres – offrant 27 types couvrant des configurations standard passe-bas, passe-haut, passe-bande et notch, des filtres vintage et de style échelle et un filtre à voyelles à changement de formants – façonnent la sortie combinée. La modulation est gérée par quatre LFO et quatre types d'enveloppes (ADSR, AHD, DADSR et DAHDSR), complétés par des générateurs aléatoires, une vélocité, une clé et une source d'aftertouch.

content_de: Das neue Plugin kombiniert resonatorbasierte akustische Emulation mit subtraktiver Synthese und ist zum Einführungspreis von 99 US-Dollar erhältlich. reFX hat Rippler veröffentlicht, ein neues Plugin, das physikalische Modellierung mit subtraktiver Synthese über zwei unabhängige Ebenen hinweg kombiniert. Das Plugin ist ab sofort für macOS 10.13 und höher verfügbar und unterstützt sowohl Apple Silicon- als auch Intel-Prozessoren sowie für Windows 10 und höher in den Formaten VST, Audio Units und AAX. Rippler wurde entwickelt, um akustische und halbakustische Klangfarben zu erzeugen, indem das physikalische Verhalten von Instrumenten wie Saiten, Röhren, Membranen und Glocken modelliert und dann der resultierende Klang mit herkömmlichen Filter- und Modulationswerkzeugen geformt wird. title_en: How To make your own kick drums in Diva
summary_en: With so many kick drum samples available, it’s easy to overlook the benefits of programming your own. It only takes seconds. Kick drums, eh? You can’t live with ‘em, but you can’t ...
content_en: With so many kick drum samples available, it’s easy to overlook the benefits of programming your own. It only takes seconds. Kick drums, eh? You can’t live with ‘em, but you can’t live without programming ‘em. Except, of course, you can – there are bloody millions of kick samples to choose from! So why bother programming your own? Three reasons, really. 1. It’s a great way to really tailor your kick to your track. 2. It helps your productions stand out. 3. It’s good for the soul to go beyond presets and make your own sounds. And… er…. 4. It’s too easy not to give it a go. STEP 1 First thing’s first: the meaty bit of pretty much every electronic kick you’ve ever used is based on applying a pitch envelope to a simple oscillator like a triangle or sine wave. That’s how the 808 did it. That’s how the 909 did it. And that’s how we’ll do it. So start by loading Diva and selecting an INIT patch. STEP 2 Now let’s configure Diva’s modules. Choose DUAL VCO (oscillators), HPF PRE (high pass filter), MULTIMODE (low pass), and Analogue (both envelopes). Then program a four-four kick pattern on F#1. And let’s use a short 1/16th length as that allows plenty of length control later. STEP 3 DCO settings next. Start with Osc1 to triangle (the 909-style layer) and Osc2 to sine (808 vibes). Then set Tune MOD mode to BOTH, to make sure the pitch envelope applies to both. And apply SYNC so both trigger together without intermittent phase cancellation between them. STEP 4 Now let’s turn it into a kick drum. First set the Tune MOD Env to fully +. Envelope 2 is now controlling the oscillator pitch so start by setting Sustain and Release to 0. See how you can hear the pitch coming down quickly already? Now slowly pull the Decay down to 32… and there’s our kick drum! STEP 5 Let’s look at the different ways of tailoring our kick next, starting with the amp envelope. First bring Sustain down to zero and then try raising Release from 20 to 50. Release is the key length control for our kick. But, as you can hear, it’s also central to the tonality of the kick, ranging from tight 909-style to tonal hardcore techno. STEP 6 The filter section is the key to adding some of that distinctive 909 kick click we all know and love. Set the lowpass Env2 amount to fully + and then start lowering the cutoff down to around 34. Now we’ve got a click. We can also try flicking the Mix between Osc1 and Osc2 to hear the difference. Osc1 is that tight, clicky 909, Osc2 is the more tonal, saturated-sounding 808 style. Filtered Filtered Osc1 Filtered Osc2 STEP 7 Finally, try tweaking the Fine Tune to adjust the tuning of the kick. And you can also experiment with different MIDI trigger note values and lengths, but that will only really make a lot of difference on kicks with longer release times for more tonality. This can be fun for edits, as you can hear below. Fine-tune up Fine-tune down Pitch edit 1 Pitch edit 2 BONUS TIP 1 You can use these kicks as a powerful sub bassline tool by layering them with another kick sample… and then raising the amplitude envelope a tiny bit. That way you have the huge bassline power of a long kick but without overloading the transient section or taking away from your chosen kick sample. But there’s a snag. Have a listen… BONUS TIP 2 As you can hear, the sound of each synth kick varies a little from the previous because their long decay tails are causing interactions with the following ones. To avoid this, render out your Diva kick and simply loop the audio over the ¼ bar section you like the sound of. Listen to how much more effective that is now… BONUS TIP 3 As we just saw, analogue synth-style kicks like this do have a tendency to have minor little variations (more or less click or slight timing / phase variations. This is the nature of analogue emulation, and can sound great in organic electronic music, but for tight, club bangers it’s often worth sampling out a single kick you’re happy with and using that for every beat instead. So there it is - a fully customisable kick with a blend of classic 808 and 909 vibes. We’ve made it in a bog-standard subtractive synth configuration in Diva, to show how easy it is, but imagine how much more detailed, individual control and processing you can get over the two oscillators with a modular or semi-modular option like Zebra 3! And don’t forget, these are all dry and unprocessed. Be sure to fire up your compressor and EQ to sharpen them up in the mix. Find out more about Diva on the u-he website, including the free trial. title_en: 5 of the Best Software and Hardware Trackers
summary_en: If you make a genre like jungle, IDM or breakcore, you need a tracker. These are the five best trackers available, plus how to bring one into your workflow. We’re all familiar with...
content_en: If you make a genre like jungle, IDM or breakcore, you need a tracker. These are the five best trackers available, plus how to bring one into your workflow. We’re all familiar with the traditional DAW sequencer, which scrolls along a timeline from left to right. Most major DAWs use some kind of horizontal sequencer, with note information represented as blocks on a piano roll, but this is not the only game in town. Trackers provide a novel alternative, one that displays note and parameter information as numbers, and proceeds vertically, tumbling from the top of the screen down. Trackers may seem confounding from the outside, but depending on your chosen genre or production style, they may provide a useful alternative to software like Ableton Live, either as a companion or wholesale replacement. Let’s take a look at five of the best trackers available today, in both software and hardware formats, and explore how you might bring a tracker into your own productions. What Is A Tracker? First, it may be helpful to clarify what a tracker is. Sometimes called a music tracker, a tracker is a sequencer that uses numbers to represent note, parameter and effect changes, with columns representing instruments and lines corresponding to note divisions. https://youtu.be/inUOTPt2mLk?si=sDaDjI_2wWI8qoPy The first tracker was Ultimate Soundtracker, released for the Commodore Amiga in 1987. This soon became the software of choice for the demoscene, with hackers creating cracktros – introduction music for their cracked software – with it. The best-known tracker, however, is OctaMED, which went through a few different iterations over its lifetime. The software was particularly popular with jungle producers like DJ Aphrodte, Bizzy B and DJ Zinc, as well as breakcore don Venetian Snares in his earlier days. Producer Pete Cannon still makes use of the software. Because of the structure of the tracker sequencer, it’s extremely easy to create pitch rolls, volume swells and other quick changes typical of genres like jungle and IDM. Aphex Twin didn’t start out on a tracker, but Drukqs, arguably the most Aphex record he did, was made with a tracker called PlayerPro. Five of the Best Trackers Given that trackers started within computer culture, it’s possible to run emulations of classic trackers like OctaMED on modern computers. If you’re really serious about old-school production methods, you can do like Pete Cannon and work with actual vintage Amigas. But for most of us, a modern tracker will be much easier to get started with. Here are five of the best that you can get right now. They’re organized in order of ascending price, with software first and hardware second. Alexander Zolotov Sunvox Free on desktop and only $5 for iOS (with AUv3 for Logic and Live included), SunVox from developer Alexander Zolotov is the cheapest way to explore a modern tracker workflow. Originally built in 2008 and based on an underlying freeware engine, SunVox is a modular software synthesizer that also happens to have a tracker sequencer built-in. https://youtu.be/xK1VMKaxGoc?si=xOJ55NvqQhl0H7E0 Like Reaktor but possibly even nerdier, it features synthesizers with subtractive, FM, sample-based, drum, and additive sound engines, plus effects and utility modules. Hook up the modules in the Module View and sequence them with the Pattern Editor. Get SunVox and find out more on the developer’s website. Electronisounds TRX-12 The tracker scene is, by its very nature, grassroots. Born out of hacker culture, trackers are often made by passionate individuals. Dean Daughters of Electronisounds is one such individual, and he’s turned love for the sequencer type into TRX-12, a new self-contained tracker DAW. TRX-12 does basic notes but it also features 35 step-FX commands. Step-FX are the secret weapons of trackers. These allow you to create per-note ratchets, glides, randomization, and other tricks that would be mind-numbingly tedious to do in a traditional DAW. https://youtu.be/-UEUkRYSTG4?si=aLIE3DvC3tcDBML2 TRX-12 includes its own instruments, with three polyphonic synthesizer engines, a multi-sample synth and two dedicated slicer tracks for break chopping. There’s a mixer with per-track sends, sidechain ducking, effects and a mastering chain, and you also get 4GB of sample content to play with. TRX-12 costs $29.99 and is available for Mac and PC. Find out more at the Electronisounds website. Renoise When it comes to modern trackers, Renoise is the reigning king. On the market since 2002 and built by a dedicated team of developers, it’s now up to version 3.5. A fully fledged DAW, it offers plugin support, built-in effects (and very good ones, too), a world-class sample slicer, meta devices for modulation, MIDI, graphical automation, and so on. There are also Tools, which add functionality to the DAW like Max for Live patches do Ableton. When you see videos online of people making music with a tracker, it’s usually Renoise. Along with its rock-solid coding and deep feature set, Renoise also offers a wealth of educational videos to help you comprehend the tracker workflow. Although the DAW does make concessions to modern music production, it’s still a tracker at heart, and so requires you to know about things like hexadecimal notation. Thankfully, whoever does their tutorials has a knack for explaining things in a clear and easy-to-understand manner. https://youtu.be/lepkIZH21Y8?si=sIXi_cjq4nn2QRsN Renoise is also extremely affordable at only $88. If you want access to the Renoise sampler (including the tracker-based sequencer) but don’t need the full DAW, check out Redux for $56 instead. Find out more at the Renoise site. Dirtywave M8 Not every tracker is software-only. Ever since some chiptune fanatics turned their Nintendo Gameboy into a tracker-based sequencer called LSDJ, the idea has been out there. Inspired by that LSDJ, Dirtywave has made M8, a portable tracker in a black box that’s equal parts groovebox and external sequencer. The sequencer part gives you eight monophonic tracks to work with (tracker channels are traditionally monophonic), 255 patterns, and a song arranger with live mode, while the instrument side includes a chiptune synth, a synthesizer based on Mutable Instruments’ Braids, an FM engine, and a sampler, along with effects. https://youtu.be/TpBIjuG5C4Q?si=ARxOtPC3_rEvlLp8 Being a hardware device, M8 is not going to be as deep as a piece of software like Renoise, but it is a fun and portable way to explore the tracker workflow - and it sounds amazing. The latest Model:02 costs $699. Find out more at the Dirtywave site. Polyend Tracker+ The original official hardware tracker was Polyend’s Tracker. Released in 2020, it brought the horizontal workflow to a groovebox format. That original device has been discontinued, with Tracker+ now replacing it. This beefed-up model offers four synth engines, a drum machine, stereo sampling and a built-in FM radio, plus 16 tracks of sequencing and audio over USB. If you like the idea of taking your tracker on the go, check out Tracker Mini. Compatible with the bigger Tracker+, the Mini throws in a battery plus an onboard microphone for field sampling. It also replaces some of the controls with a video game-style D-pad, bringing that old-school computer and gaming connection to the forefront. https://youtu.be/iQCwD3wNlhE?si=Fz_uDFwiezEUMFHc Tracker+ is $999 while the Tracker Mini will set you back $799. Get more information on the Polyend site. Trackers In Use How easy is it to make music with a tracker? It’s honestly not all that hard. There is, of course, a learning curve, but if you approach it like learning any new DAW, you’ll probably find things falling into place pretty quickly. In some ways, trackers are faster than regular DAWs. The focus, at least for something like Renoise, is on the computer keyboard, so you may even find yourself leaving MIDI behind and working entirely with QWERTY keys instead. Here’s an example of a track we whipped up in Renoise. It’s got two chopped breaks, sampled kick and snare one-shots, and a Reese sample and transition sound, all sourced from sounds that came with the DAW. There’s also Rave Generator 2 in there. The effects are a mix of native ones, both as inserts on tracks and built into the sampler, as well as third-party plugins like FabFilter Pro-Q 4 and D16 Group Frontier. Renoise jungle: Lastly, there’s nothing that says you can only do fast-paced music with a tracker. Lots of people do house, techno and other, more straightforward genres with it. It’s whatever you feel most comfortable with. content_es: Si haces un género como Jungle, IDM o Breakcore, necesitas un rastreador. Estos son los cinco mejores rastreadores disponibles, además de cómo incorporar uno a su flujo de trabajo. Todos estamos familiarizados con el secuenciador DAW tradicional, que se desplaza a lo largo de una línea de tiempo de izquierda a derecha. La mayoría de los principales DAW utilizan algún tipo de secuenciador horizontal, con la información de las notas representada como bloques en un rollo de piano, pero este no es el único juego que existe. Los rastreadores ofrecen una alternativa novedosa, una que muestra información de notas y parámetros como números y avanza verticalmente, cayendo desde la parte superior de la pantalla hacia abajo. Los rastreadores pueden parecer confusos desde fuera, pero dependiendo del género o estilo de producción elegido, pueden proporcionar una alternativa útil a software como Ableton Live, ya sea como complemento o reemplazo total. Echemos un vistazo a cinco de los mejores rastreadores disponibles en la actualidad, tanto en formato de software como de hardware, y exploremos cómo puedes incorporar un rastreador a tus propias producciones. ¿Qué es un rastreador? En primer lugar, puede resultar útil aclarar qué es un rastreador. A veces llamado rastreador de música, un rastreador es un secuenciador que utiliza números para representar cambios de notas, parámetros y efectos, con columnas que representan instrumentos y líneas correspondientes a divisiones de notas. https://youtu.be/inUOTPt2mLk?si=sDaDjI_2wWI8qoPy El primer tracker fue Ultimate Soundtracker, lanzado para Commodore Amiga en 1987. Pronto se convirtió en el software elegido para la escena de demostración, con los hackers creando cracktros (música de introducción para su software crackeado) con él. Sin embargo, el rastreador más conocido es OctaMED, que pasó por algunas iteraciones diferentes a lo largo de su vida. El software fue particularmente popular entre productores de la jungla como DJ Aphrodte, Bizzy B y DJ Zinc, así como también con el don del breakcore Venetian Snares en sus primeros días. El productor Pete Cannon todavía utiliza el software. Debido a la estructura del secuenciador de seguimiento, es extremadamente fácil crear cambios de tono, aumentos de volumen y otros cambios rápidos.
